item.title: Lake Biwa Cruises: Paddlewheelers and Island Boats — Guide
item.description: Cruising is the classic way to feel the sheer scale of Lake Biwa, and the lake runs a whole fleet for it. From Otsu near Kyoto sails the Michigan, an American-style paddlewheeler offering sightseeing, lunch and dinner cruises with live music along the southern lake; from the northern ports of Nagahama and Imazu, pilgrimage ferries cross to the sacred island of Chikubushima; and seasonal boats run to beaches and viewpoints around the shore.

item.title: Lake Biwa Fireworks: Summer Nights Over Otsu — Guide
item.description: The Lake Biwa Great Fireworks Festival, held on an evening in early August off Otsu, is one of the Kansai region’s biggest summer displays: some 10,000 shells burst over the open lake, their colours mirrored in the broad dark water and reflected off the lakeside towers of Otsu, drawing hundreds of thousands of spectators to the shore. Because the launches are over water with no obstructions, the shells hang huge and clear above the lake, and the setting — Japan’s largest lake, an easy ten minutes from Kyoto — makes it one of the most accessible major hanabi for visitors based in the old capital.

item.title: Lake Biwa: Japan's Largest and Oldest Lake — Guide
item.description: Lake Biwa is the vast heart of Shiga — Japan’s largest freshwater lake, covering roughly a sixth of the entire prefecture, and one of the oldest lakes on Earth at some four million years, old enough to have evolved dozens of species found nowhere else. It supplies drinking water to the whole Kansai region and shapes life around its 235-kilometre shoreline, where beaches, marinas, cruise piers, cycling paths and lakeside shrines ring waters that turn from morning mirror-calm to windsurfing chop.
